title: Application and Infrastructure Deployment on Google Cloud
bodyMarkdown:
# Application and Infrastructure Deployment

An architect advising dev and ops teams is judged on one thing: can a change get from a commit to production repeatedly, safely, and reversibly? This module covers the Google Cloud delivery toolchain (build, store, deliver, run), the deployment strategies each runtime supports, and the testing layers that gate each step. The recurring exam theme is **choosing the purpose-built managed service** and **promoting one immutable artifact through environments**.

## The delivery chain and who owns which step

A pipeline has four distinct jobs, and each has a Google Cloud product that is the "default answer":

| Stage | Product | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Source and trigger | GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Cloud Storage; Cloud Build triggers | A push, pull request, Pub/Sub message, or webhook starts a build |
| Build and test (CI) | **Cloud Build** | Runs a series of steps, each in its own container, and produces artifacts |
| Store | **Artifact Registry** | Holds container images and language packages; integrates with Artifact Analysis for vulnerability scanning |
| Deliver (CD) | **Cloud Deploy** | Promotes a release through an ordered sequence of targets with approvals, verification, canary, and rollback |
| Run | Cloud Run, GKE, Compute Engine MIGs | Executes the workload |

[Cloud Build](https://cloud.google.com/build/docs/overview) executes a build config file (typically `cloudbuild.yaml`) as "a series of build steps, where each build step is run in a Docker container." Steps can be official, community, or custom builders. Triggers cover GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Pub/Sub, and webhook events, and [private pools](https://cloud.google.com/build/docs/overview) give dedicated, fully managed workers with private network access that scale to zero.

Concrete knobs from the [build config schema](https://cloud.google.com/build/docs/build-config-file-schema) worth remembering:

- **Timeout**: default 60 minutes, maximum 24 hours. A step with no timeout runs until it finishes or the build times out.
- **Machine type**: the default is `e2-standard-2` (2 CPUs); four high-CPU types are available (two with 8 CPUs, two with 32 CPUs). Pay for bigger workers only when build time is the bottleneck.
- **`images`** pushes Docker images to Artifact Registry; **`artifacts`** stores other outputs in Cloud Storage or Artifact Registry after all steps succeed.
- **`waitFor`** expresses step dependencies so independent steps run in parallel; **`substitutions`** parameterize the config; **`serviceAccount`** selects the identity the build runs as.

[Artifact Registry](https://cloud.google.com/artifact-registry/docs/overview) is the recommended container registry. It offers four repository types: standard (direct storage), remote (caches an upstream public source), connector (proxies upstream without caching, for full auditability), and virtual (groups remote and private repositories behind a single endpoint with priority ordering). Virtual repositories are the answer when a question wants "one endpoint for both our private packages and cached public ones."

## Cloud Build vs. Cloud Deploy

These are complementary. Cloud Build owns CI; Cloud Deploy owns CD.

| Concern | Cloud Build | Cloud Deploy |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Build, test, package | Progressive delivery and promotion |
| Unit of work | Build steps in a build config | Delivery pipeline, targets, releases, rollouts |
| Approvals | Not first-class | Can be required on any target |
| Canary and rollback | You script it | Built in |
| Runtime targets | Anything you can script | GKE, Cloud Run, GKE attached clusters, custom targets |

[Cloud Deploy](https://cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/overview) "automates delivery of your applications to a series of target environments in a defined promotion sequence." A **delivery pipeline** defines the promotion order; a **target** is an environment; a **release** is the rendered manifest for each target (rendered via Skaffold from `skaffold.yaml`); a **rollout** associates a release with one target. Approval can be required for any target, and a Pub/Sub message lets an external system drive the approval. [Promotion](https://cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/promote-release) with `gcloud deploy releases promote` goes to the next target in the sequence unless `--to-target` is given.

**Rollback** in Cloud Deploy is not an undo button; it [creates a new rollout](https://cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/roll-back) from a previous release. By default it uses the last release with a successful rollout to that target, or a specific one via `--release`.

**Verification** is built in: after deployment, Cloud Deploy [runs your test containers](https://cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/verify-deployment). An exit code of 0 means success; any non-zero code fails verification, and a failed verification fails the rollout. If several containers run, all must succeed.

## Deployment strategies

| Strategy | How it works | Where it is native on Google Cloud |
|---|---|---|
| Rolling | Replace instances gradually | Managed instance groups, Kubernetes Deployments |
| Blue/green | Build a parallel environment, then switch traffic | Cloud Run revisions with traffic shift; load balancer backend swap |
| Canary | Send a small share of traffic to the new version, watch metrics, then widen | Cloud Deploy canary; Cloud Run traffic split; MIG canary update |

### Canary in Cloud Deploy

A [canary deployment](https://cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/deployment-strategies/canary) splits traffic between the deployed version and the new one. The rollout contains one phase per increment plus a final `stable` phase at 100%. Increments of 25, 50, and 75 percent create phases `canary-25`, `canary-50`, `canary-75`, and `stable`. There are three modes: **automated** (Cloud Deploy apportions traffic), **custom-automated** (you name phases and Skaffold profiles; Cloud Deploy balances), and **custom** (you control everything, works for all target types). Supported runtimes are GKE (and attached clusters), Cloud Run services and worker pools (not jobs), and custom targets. A subtle limit: with the GKE Gateway API, a canary phase may be 100%, but for GKE service-based canaries, attached clusters, and Cloud Run, percentages cannot reach 100% before the final `stable` phase. Deploy analysis can use Google Cloud Observability metrics and automation rules can advance the rollout automatically.

### Cloud Run traffic management

[Cloud Run revisions](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/rollouts-rollbacks-traffic-migration) are immutable snapshots of code and configuration. You can split traffic across revisions, but percentages across active revisions must total 100. A **gradual rollout** deploys with no traffic, then raises the share (for example starting around 5%) as metrics hold. A **rollback** is sending 100% to an earlier revision. **Traffic tags** give a revision its own URL, such as `https://tag-name---service-abcdef.a.run.app`, so you can test before production traffic arrives. Traffic splits persist across future deployments until you reset them, which is a classic surprise: a new deploy may not receive traffic you expected.

### MIG rolling updates

For VM workloads, [managed instance group updates](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instance-groups/rolling-out-updates-to-managed-instance-groups) come in two types: **proactive** (automatic; the MIG applies the new template to all or a subset of VMs) and **opportunistic** (applied only when you act or when autoscaling or resizing creates new VMs). `maxSurge` and `maxUnavailable` default to 1 multiplied by the number of affected zones. Setting `maxUnavailable` to 0 with a positive `maxSurge` keeps full capacity during the update at the cost of extra billed instances. Automated updates support up to two instance template versions at once, which is how you do a MIG canary.

## Choosing a runtime

[Cloud Run](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/overview/what-is-cloud-run) is a fully managed platform; services scale automatically and scale to zero when idle. It also offers jobs, worker pools, and functions. Choose it when the workload is containerized, request-driven or batch, and the team wants minimal infrastructure management. Choose **GKE** when you need Kubernetes-native features, complex orchestration, or cluster-level control. Choose **Compute Engine MIGs** for VM-based or lift-and-shift workloads that cannot be containerized yet.

## Infrastructure goes through the same pipeline

Infrastructure changes follow the same discipline as application changes: version-controlled definitions, a reviewable plan, automated apply, and promotion through environments. Module 4 covers Terraform, state, and Infrastructure Manager in depth. The [DevOps capabilities from DORA](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/devops/devops-tech-test-automation) (continuous delivery, deployment automation, test automation, trunk-based development) are the framing Google uses for why this matters.

## Test layers that gate the pipeline

Put most tests at the base of the pyramid. **Unit tests** run in seconds on every commit with mocked dependencies; they are the first gate in Cloud Build. **Integration tests** exercise components together (often against local emulators, see module 5) and run on merge. **End-to-end tests** are few, slow, and run against a deployed environment, which in Cloud Deploy is exactly what the verify step is for. Load and stress tests are pre-launch gates, not per-commit checks (module 3).

## Anti-patterns and common mistakes

- **Rebuilding per environment.** Building a fresh image for staging and again for prod means prod runs something nobody tested. Build once, push to Artifact Registry, promote the same digest.
- **Scripting promotion in Cloud Build with `kubectl apply` to every cluster.** It works until you need approvals, a canary phase, verification, or a rollback audit trail; then you are rebuilding Cloud Deploy by hand.
- **Mutable tags such as `latest`.** Rollback and reproducibility both depend on immutable identifiers.
- **No tested rollback path.** Rollback in Cloud Deploy is a new rollout, so confirm the previous release still renders and deploys.
- **Using canary without metrics.** A canary phase with no deploy analysis or monitoring is just a slow release.
- **Forgetting that Cloud Run traffic splits persist.** After a manual 90/10 split, later deploys do not automatically take 100%.
- **Giving every build the broadest identity.** Use the `serviceAccount` field with least-privilege roles rather than a project-wide editor identity.
- **Nightly redeploys on a schedule** (Cloud Scheduler, cron) as a substitute for pipeline-driven promotion; it has no gates, no approvals, and no per-commit traceability.

## Exam tips

- **Purpose-built CD is Cloud Deploy.** "Progressive delivery, ordered dev/staging/prod targets, approvals, canary, one-click rollback" points to Cloud Deploy, not Cloud Build triggers running `kubectl apply`.
- **Build is not deliver.** Cloud Build is CI (build, test, package); Cloud Deploy is CD (promote, approve, verify, roll back). Pick the one that matches the verb in the question.
- **Promote the same artifact.** Rebuilding per environment is wrong; push one immutable image to Artifact Registry and promote it.
- **Know the canary runtimes.** Cloud Deploy canary works on GKE, Cloud Run services (not jobs), and custom targets; Cloud Run itself also splits traffic by revision percentage.
- **Cloud Run rollback is traffic, not redeploy.** Send 100% of traffic to an earlier revision; traffic tags let you test a revision at its own URL first.
- **Rollback in Cloud Deploy creates a new rollout** from the last successfully deployed release unless you name another.
- **Unit tests are the base of the pyramid.** The fastest per-commit feedback comes from unit tests; end-to-end and load tests are few and run later.
- **VM fleets use MIG updates.** Proactive versus opportunistic, `maxSurge`/`maxUnavailable`, and two template versions for a canary are the vocabulary to recognize.
